newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says optimistic on oil exploration.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says optimistic on oil exploration.

text.p: Indonesian Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana said on Monday he was optimistic that his country was still attractive for foreign oil investors, although no new incentives were being offered.
"The intention of foreign oil investors to explore in Indonesia is still high. I am optimistic that the trend will continue in future," Sudjana said.

He was speaking after signing extensions to oil production contracts between state oil company Pertamina and several foreign companies, including Santa Fe Energy Resources Inc and Asamera Overseas Limited, a subsidiary of Gulf Canada Resources Ltd
"We are not considering new incentives at the moment because we see that foreign investment is still high. Indonesia still has potential for hydrocarbon resources," Sudjana told reporters.
Existing incentives are for exploration in high-risk frontier areas, including Irian Jaya, where contractors can receive 35 percent of oil output from any find as opposed to 20 percent elsewhere.
OPEC member Indonesia currently produces around 1.60 million barrels per day of crude oil and condensate.
Pertamina's director of Exploration Prijambodo Muljosudirdjo said he hoped current high oil prices would boost exploration activities in Indonesia.
"Oil prices currently are quite high and I hope exploration activities will increase," Muljosudirdjo told reporters.
Sudjana asked Pertamina to increase cooperation with foreign oil conntractors in order to boost efficiency.
Pertamina said on Monday it had extended oil production contracts with Santa Fe and Asamera for 20 years each.
Muljosudirdjo told reporters that the Santa Fe contract, relating to an offshore block in Irian Jaya province, would be extended until 2020.
The Asamera contract, relating to a block in South Sumatra would be extended until 2023, he said.
Muljosudirdjo also said Pertamina signed three new oil-production contracts on Monday.
One, for the Sibolga block offshore northern Sumatra, was signed with U.S. oil major Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, he said. No details of the contracts were immediately available.
Another contract had been signed with Eurafrep Nederland BV for an onshore block in central Java, Muljosudirdjo said.
A third contract, with Canadian Petroleum Indonesia Ltd, was signed for an offshore block in the Molucca Islands, he said.
Pertamina also signed two technical assistance contracts with local companies PT Garis Astra Tunggal and PT Pilona Petro Tanjung but details were not given.
Most major oil companies are engaged in exploration in Indonesia, including Mobil Corp, Chevron, Texaco, and Atlantic Richfield Co. At least 20 production-sharing contracts were signed in 1995.
